summary:
Ekiti State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe' records enforcement and violence specific to the state. On 21 January 2014, days after the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened her with 'You will get 14 years in prison!'; the report states she was beaten at least twice over the period.

Debbie was unable to use Ekiti's health services safely and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, indicating that trans and HIV-positive residents in the state face care access barriers that push them to seek treatment in Oyo State.

The report also documents police and official conduct in Ado Ekiti: in September 2014 a gay man was arrested at the Faguyi bar in the state capital, his third arrest, and was released after two days in detention once he paid 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend. In a separate 2014 incident, a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.
tangentialFactors:
Extortion and payment for release appear as documented features of Ekiti enforcement: the September 2014 Faguyi bar arrest ended only after a combined 12,000 Naira payment, and a state investigator separately extorted a young gay man in Ado Ekiti in 2014. Visitors who are read as LGBT+ in the state should expect that any police contact may carry a financial demand.

The violence documented against Debbie in Ado Ekiti was carried out by private individuals invoking the SSMPA's 14-year penalty as a threat, a pattern consistent with the national picture of the law being used to justify assault by non-state actors.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ekiti State face documented barriers to health care on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Debbie's case shows that HIV treatment could not be obtained locally without risk, requiring a six-hour round trip to Ibadan; whether Ekiti's public health facilities have since changed practice is not addressed in the sources.

State investigators in Ado Ekiti have used their position to extort gay residents, and repeated arrest of the same individual was recorded within a single year, indicating that prior police contact does not end the exposure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not resolve whether Ekiti State has any state-level legislation on same-sex conduct or cross-dressing distinct from the national SSMPA, or whether the state has its own hate-crime or anti-discrimination provisions covering gender identity.

No information is available in the inventory on the current operation of Ekiti's correctional or remand facilities with respect to transgender detainees, on the state's police command directives regarding gender-nonconforming people, or on whether the health-service access problem documented in 2016 has been addressed.

The outcome of the Faguyi bar arrests and of the 2014 extortion complaint against the state investigator is not sourced.
